title: Sufism
summary: Sufi seems first to have meant one who wears wool: in the eighth century the name was given to Muslim ascetics in coarse woollen garments. Ascetic circles in Iraq, especially Basra, Kufa and Baghdad, and in Khorasan and Egypt grew in the eighth and ninth centuries into a mysticism of selfless love for God, voiced by Rabi'a al-Adawiyya. From about the twelfth century Sufi orders such as the Qadiriyya spread across the Islamic world, and Sufi poets such as Rumi shaped its literature.

uncertainty.note: Early ascetic roots emerged in the eighth century (c. 750–800 CE) and coalesced into formal tasawwuf in the ninth century.

as_recorded.value: In the eighth century the word was sometimes being applied to Muslims whose ascetic inclinations led them to wear coarse and uncomfortable woolen garments
The three major centers of the ascetic movement in the eighth and ninth centuries were Iraq, especially the cities of Basra, Kufa, and Baghdad

where.modern_name: Baghdad, Iraq (early center of classical Sufi schools)

importance.justification: Became the main form of Islamic mysticism and, through its orders, a mainstay of Muslim piety and social life across the Islamic world (R3 D2 T4 L3).
